rfm_tuples.R: Our Distilling Solutions segment is subject to unfavorable macro industry trends... [yet] aging whiskey inventory [is a strategic strength]. The brown goods decline was primarily the result of softening American whiskey category trends and elevated industry-wide barrel inventories, leading to softer than expected spot sales, and instances of customer contract non-performance.
rfm_tuples.f: Cross-check internal narrative against actual barreled-distillate inventory build. If destocking is industry-wide and customers are walking from contracts, inventory should be cut, not grown.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Note 2 (Other Balance Sheet Captions) -- Inventory roll
rfm_tuples.M_value: Barreled distillate inventory grew from $250,183K (2023) to $283,119K (2024), +13.2%, while brown goods sales fell -8% and Distilling Solutions segment sales fell -26%. Operating cash flow note confirms $18,155K use-of-cash in 2024 'related to an increase in inventories, primarily barreled distillate' (and prior year was $46,921K of the same).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: classic build-into-weakness. Management acknowledges industry oversupply and customer non-performance but continued to lay down barrels at the customer-of-yourself, betting demand returns. This is the same pattern that converted weakness into goodwill impairment + class-action liability.

rfm_tuples.R: We have been, and may continue to be, adversely impacted by elevated industry-wide barrel inventories of whiskey... customer contract non-performance, which we have experienced in the past, could adversely impact our business.
rfm_tuples.f: Compare risk-factor disclosure to the timing of the class-period start date (May 4, 2023) implied by the two securities class actions filed against the company.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 3 / Note 10 Commitments and Contingencies (Operating Engineers Action filed Dec 16, 2024; Bronstein Action filed Feb 13, 2025)
rfm_tuples.M_value: Both putative securities class actions cover the period May 4, 2023 - October 30, 2024 (17 months) and allege false/misleading statements under 10(b)/20(a). Filed pre-cutoff. A derivative suit (Sebald v. Colo) additionally alleges the board breached fiduciary duty by 'causing the Company to repurchase its own stock at artificially inflated prices.'
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode A confirms: the 'risk factor' language is post-hoc euphemism for a 17-month period of disclosures that two separate plaintiffs' firms believe were materially misleading. The October 30, 2024 class-period end-point identifies the negative-disclosure catalyst that the 10-K does not narratively highlight.

rfm_tuples.R: On February 29, 2024, we announced that our Board of Directors approved a $100,000 share repurchase program... During the year ended December 31, 2024, we repurchased 886,936 shares of Common Stock for approximately $46,588 [thousand].
rfm_tuples.f: Time the actual buyback execution against the October 30, 2024 negative-disclosure date (the class-period terminus). If management knew distress was emerging, accelerating buybacks at $45-49 just AFTER the disclosure looks like value-destruction or signaling support of an artificial price.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 5 (Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities) -- Q4 2024 monthly repurchase table
rfm_tuples.M_value: Oct 2024: 0 shares. Nov 2024: 557,552 shares @ $49.09 avg. Dec 2024: 201,024 shares @ $45.86 avg. Total Q4: 758,576 shares for ~$36.6M -- 78% of the full-year buyback executed in the two months AFTER the Oct 30, 2024 disclosure that capped the securities class period. Cutoff price (5/15/2025): $33.56. Forward price (5/15/2026): $18.05.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: capital allocation pattern is a tell. Acceleration of buybacks immediately AFTER the Oct 30 disclosure that triggered class actions is exactly what the derivative complaint alleges (buying at 'artificially inflated prices'). Either (a) management did not believe the weakness was structural -- they were wrong, -46% forward -- or (b) buybacks were used to defend a price the insiders knew was overstated. Both readings are bearish.

rfm_tuples.R: On December 3, 2024, Karen L. Seaberg, a member of our Board of Directors, amended a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan... [and on] December 3, 2024, Lori S. Mingus, a member... amended a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan... In each case, the amendment revised the price terms of the Rule 10b5-1 trading plan.
rfm_tuples.f: Cluster insider 10b5-1 amendments against the same Oct 30, 2024 disclosure catalyst. Are two directors lowering price thresholds (i.e., now willing to sell into lower prices) within ~5 weeks of the disclosure that triggered the class actions?
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 9B (Other Information) -- Director and Officer Trading Arrangements
rfm_tuples.M_value: Two long-tenured directors (Seaberg, Mingus -- both Cray-family-linked legacy holders given the Cloud L. Cray Sr. founding) simultaneously amended price terms of pre-existing 10b5-1 plans on the same day (Dec 3, 2024), 34 days after the Oct 30 disclosure and 13 days before the first class action was filed. Seaberg plan covers up to $8,735K, Mingus up to $643K, both running through May 31, 2025 -- i.e., disposing into and through the cutoff window.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: synchronized insider 10b5-1 amendments at directors who collectively trace to the founding family, timed within weeks of a disclosure catalyst, with revised price terms (almost certainly lowering trigger floors so they sell sooner/lower) is the textbook insider-vs-calendar tell. The 10-K discloses the existence but not the direction of the price-term revisions.

rfm_tuples.R: Goodwill impairment 73,755 [thousand]... As a result of the quantitative goodwill impairment test, we recorded an impairment charge of $73,755 to adjust the carrying amount of the Branded Spirits reporting unit to fair value... Change in fair value of contingent consideration 16,100 [versus 7,100 prior year, related to Penelope].
rfm_tuples.f: Reconcile the goodwill writedown against the simultaneous up-mark of Penelope contingent consideration. If Branded Spirits is impaired, does it make sense for Penelope (sitting inside Branded Spirits) to be MORE likely to hit earn-out targets?
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Consolidated Statement of Income / Note 4 Contingent Consideration
rfm_tuples.M_value: Branded Spirits goodwill: written down $73.8M in Q4 2024. Simultaneously, Penelope contingent consideration liability MARKED UP from $69.2M to $85.3M ($16.1M up-mark), implying management raised projected Penelope net sales through Dec 31, 2025 even as the reporting unit it sits inside was being impaired. Earn-out cap is $110.8M -- so management is now modeling Penelope at ~77% of max attainment.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B contradiction. Internal model has Penelope accelerating while the broader Branded Spirits unit's fair value collapses -- a Monte Carlo input choice flagged by KPMG as a critical audit matter. If Penelope misses, the contingent consideration unwinds (a 2026 positive) but signals further organic weakness; if Penelope hits, cash outflow of up to $110.8M lands in 2026 against a stressed balance sheet ($317M total debt, $105M variable-rate revolver due 2026).

rfm_tuples.R: Revenue recognition under bill and hold arrangements... the Company's Distilling Solutions segment routinely enters into bill and hold arrangements, whereby the Company produces and sells aged and unaged distillate to customers... brown goods revenue was $265,873 thousand for the year ended December 31, 2024, a portion of which was for bill and hold arrangements. We identified the evaluation of revenue recognized under bill and hold arrangements as a critical audit matter.
rfm_tuples.f: Quantify the share of brown goods revenue that is bill-and-hold. The 10-K omits the percentage; KPMG flags it as critical audit matter.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Note 1 (Revenue Recognition) + KPMG Critical Audit Matter section
rfm_tuples.M_value: Bill-and-hold portion of $265.9M brown-goods revenue is NOT disclosed in dollars or percentage. KPMG required additional audit effort to verify the four bill-and-hold criteria (substantive reason, separately identified inventory, ready for transfer, no ability to use for another customer). Combined with the simultaneous $33M build in barreled distillate inventory and instances of customer contract non-performance, bill-and-hold revenue is the line item to watch.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode A: claim is intentionally non-quantitative on a high-risk revenue mechanism. Bill-and-hold + customer non-performance + inventory build is a known pre-restatement combination (e.g., Diageo SEC settlement 2020 for whiskey channel-stuffing-adjacent practices). Cannot confirm fraud, but the disclosure pattern is consistent with channel pressure on a maturing-stock segment.

rfm_tuples.R: During 2024, one customer of the Branded Spirits segment accounted for approximately 13 percent of our consolidated sales... During 2024, one customer of the Ingredient Solutions segment accounted for approximately 12 percent of our consolidated sales... ten largest customers accounted for approximately 53 percent [vs] 44 percent [2023] and 38 percent [2022].
rfm_tuples.f: Track concentration trajectory. Rising customer concentration in a destocking environment is a leverage-to-loss signal: if the 13% distributor renegotiates terms, mid-teens % of revenue is at risk.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Top-10 customer share rose from 38% (2022) -> 44% (2023) -> 53% (2024) -- +15pp in 2 years. Two single customers now at ~13% and ~12% of CONSOLIDATED revenue. Three-tier US distribution consolidation acknowledged in risk factors but not quantified.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: rising concentration is the mathematical consequence of a shrinking denominator (sales -16% YoY) more than absolute customer growth. Either way, the 2025 contract cycle for two ~12-13% customers is the swing variable -- and the company has just acknowledged 'instances of customer contract non-performance.'

rfm_tuples.R: On December 31, 2024, David S. Bratcher's service as our Chief Executive Officer and President ended, and Brandon M. Gall was appointed to serve as our Interim President and Chief Executive Officer effective January 1, 2025, in addition to serving in his current role of CFO.
rfm_tuples.f: Check timing of CEO exit against the Oct 30 disclosure and class-action filings. A CEO departing 60 days after the disclosure that triggered class actions, with no permanent successor named, is a high-discrimination signal.
rfm_tuples.M_value: CEO Bratcher exited Dec 31, 2024 -- 62 days after the Oct 30 disclosure catalyst and 15 days after the first class action was filed. CFO is doing double duty as Interim CEO into the 10-K filing date (Feb 26, 2025) and through the cutoff (May 15, 2025) -- 4.5 months without naming a permanent CEO. Bratcher was himself only appointed CEO in 2023 (the 10-K notes 'CEO transition' costs in 2022 SG&A growth).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: this is the third CEO transition in ~3 years. Forced or hastened exits cluster around disclosure events; the 10-K filing acknowledges Bratcher is named in both putative class actions. No replacement at the 10-K date is itself a governance red flag, and the same CFO now signs both Interim CEO and CFO certifications -- weakening the second-pair-of-eyes 302/906 control.

rfm_tuples.R: Long-term debt, less current maturities 121,277 [vs] 85,305 [prior year]; Convertible senior notes 195,864 [1.88% due 2041]; Credit Agreement - Revolver, 5.52% (variable rate) due 2026 $105,000 [vs $63,000]; Contingent consideration 85,300.
rfm_tuples.f: Test refinancing runway. Revolver matures 2026 inside the post-cutoff window, into a stressed business -- check whether amendments, waivers, or covenant relief language appears.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Revolver balance grew from $63M to $105M (+67%) at 5.52% variable, maturing 2026 (12-18 months post-cutoff). Plus $85.3M Penelope earn-out potentially due 2026 (up to $110.8M cap). Plus convertible at par. Net long-term debt rose from $280.8M to $317.1M while operating income fell 50%. No covenant amendment disclosed yet, but management's standard 'we met those covenants' language is present.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: 2026 is the cliff -- revolver maturity AND earn-out crystallization in the same year, both into deteriorating EBITDA. Buybacks of $48.8M in 2024 directly subtracted from the cash buffer needed for the 2026 refi. The 10-K does not project covenant headroom under the 2024 run-rate operating income.

rfm_tuples.R: [KPMG LLP] We have served as the Company's auditor since 2008. [No Item 9 changes/disagreements; clean Big 4; ICFR effective.]
rfm_tuples.M_value: KPMG since 2008 (17-year tenure). Big 4. Clean opinion. No 8-K Item 4.01 events. Internal controls assessed effective. Two critical audit matters (bill-and-hold, contingent consideration) but no material weakness or going-concern paragraph.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Auditor history is genuinely clean; no Mode A flag here. The discrimination comes from the other tuples, not from auditor turnover. Goodwill impairment + class actions did NOT trigger an auditor change.

summary: MGPI is a Mode-B-heavy detection: deterministic scanners correctly returned NO_GOING_CONCERN and CLEAN_BIG4_TENURE (KPMG since 2008), so a Mode-A-only framework would have scored this name as benign and missed the -46% draw. The Mode B cluster, however, is unusually dense and entirely sourced from inside the 10-K itself: management built barreled-distillate inventory +13% into an admitted industry destocking with customer contract non-performance; the Board accelerated 78% of the FY24 buyback into Nov/Dec 2024 at $46-49 per share immediately AFTER the Oct 30 disclosure that caps both putative securities class-action periods; two long-tenured directors synchronously amended 10b5-1 plans on Dec 3, 2024 to 'revise price terms'; the CEO exited 62 days after the same disclosure with no permanent successor at the 10-K date; Branded Spirits goodwill was written down $73.8M while the Penelope earn-out sitting INSIDE Branded Spirits was marked UP $16.1M (a Monte-Carlo input choice KPMG flagged as a critical audit matter); and bill-and-hold revenue on the brown-goods segment is the second critical audit matter. Two putative securities class actions plus a derivative suit alleging 'repurchase at artificially inflated prices' had already been filed pre-cutoff. The framework's correct verdict is that MGPI was not lying about distress in a forward-looking sense (no going-concern), but was obscuring the severity and timing of the demand collapse, and capital-allocating in a way that the market (and plaintiffs) read as artificial price support. Composite should be SEVERE.
